text.short: Northern Nevada pours a Picon into a six-ounce stemmed glass. Two of them exist: a stock restaurant glass everyone can buy, and a custom one made in Sparks.
text.note: Outside northern Nevada the drink lands in a highball or a Collins, which changes the proportions more than people admit — the stem glass holds six ounces, and a Collins holds twice that.

sections.heading: The one you can buy
sections.body: A Libbey 8054, the Georgian Irish coffee glass: six ounces, a slightly contoured bowl, a rimmed stem over a wide foot. It is a stock item at restaurant suppliers, which is why it is the glass most bars actually use — availability decided this, not design.

sections.heading: The one made for it
sections.body: The Louie Picon Glass Company of Sparks, Nevada, incorporated in 2009, makes a custom stemmed glass for the drink. It is a two-person business. A directory listing puts its annual revenue near $110,000, which is the scale of the whole enterprise: one small firm in one town, making the glass for one cocktail.

sections.heading: Why it matters to what you are handed
sections.body: A six-ounce stem forces the build tight — amer, a spoon of grenadine, a short top of soda, a float of brandy, a twist. Poured into a twelve-ounce Collins the same measures need lengthening, and what arrives is a longer, weaker drink wearing the same name. When people say the Picon is different away from Reno, part of what they are tasting is the glassware.
